Oral and maxillofacial surgery · published research

Sinus lift surgery

Human studies report inconsistent bone-density, bone-maturation, and postoperative symptom findings. Two 2026 titles describe the same 20-participant randomized cohort, so they are not independent trials.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Human studies report inconsistent bone-density, bone-maturation, and postoperative symptom findings. Two 2026 titles describe the same 20-participant randomized cohort, so they are not independent trials.

Summary of the Evidence

Seven human publications cover six cohorts: two direct sinus-lift RCTs and five mapped maxillary sinus-floor augmentation reports; two Dominiak papers report the same 20-participant trial. One sheep experiment is listed in a related implant-stability category. No in-vitro study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

The 44-person LED trial found no significant bone-quality or mineralized-area benefit; a 10-person Nd:YAG RCT reported less swelling and improved oral-health quality of life. Mapped trials were mixed: small studies reported greater density or bone maturation, while 12- and 20-participant cohorts found no significant new-bone advantage (Arshad et al., 2021; Ozturan et al., 2015; Mehdiyev et al., 2019; Theodoro et al., 2018; Klassmann et al., 2023; Dominiak et al., 2026). The two Dominiak 2026 papers are publications from the same 20-participant randomized cohort, not independent trials. The other mapped maxillary-augmentation reports concern related sinus-floor graft procedures but do not all use the same graft materials, irradiation schedules, or endpoints; their outcomes should not be pooled informally.

Primary original study: Dominiak et al., 2026, Effect of low-level laser therapy on healing after sinus floor augmentation using allograft and xenograft bone materials.. PubMed

Animal evidence

In sheep, laser did not improve bone regeneration in the sinus graft, though possible osseointegration effects were noted (Jakse et al., 2007).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The cited randomized report used a 635 nm diode laser at 6 J/cm² as an adjunct to sinus-floor augmentation. 635 nm is visible red light. The paired 2026 publications report the same trial cohort. Other mapped reports use different grafts and schedules, so the cited parameters should not be generalized to every sinus-lift procedure. Visible red and blue wavelengths are distinct from near-infrared wavelengths.

Interpretation

The evidence suggests possible short-term symptom or maturation effects in selected settings, but it does not show a consistent advantage in new-bone outcomes. Publications should be separated from participant cohorts, and mapped augmentation studies should not be treated as direct replications when graft materials and endpoints differ.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow. Small randomized sinus-augmentation studies report mixed bone and symptom outcomes.
Publications and records8 unique titles, comprising 7 human reports and 1 mapped sheep experiment.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several human randomized reports address sinus-floor augmentation, but the publications include overlapping participants and different graft materials and outcomes. Some report changes in density or symptoms, while others find no clear bone-regeneration advantage. One related sheep experiment is preclinical evidence, not a human outcome. A single effect estimate is not supported.
